verses.text: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
He was with God in the beginning.
Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made.
In Him was life, and that life was the light of men.
The Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it.
There came a man who was sent from God. His name was John.
He came as a witness to testify about the Light, so that through him everyone might believe.
He himself was not the Light, but he came to testify about the Light.
The true Light, who gives light to everyone, was coming into the world.
He was in the world, and though the world was made through Him, the world did not recognize Him.
He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him.
But to all who did receive Him, to those who believed in His name, He gave the right to become children of God—
children born not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but born of God.
The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.
John testified concerning Him. He cried out, saying, "This is He of whom I said, 'He who comes after me has surpassed me because He was before me.'"
From His fullness we have all received grace upon grace.
For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.
No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known.
And this was John's testimony when the Jews of Jerusalem sent priests and Levites to ask him, "Who are you?"
He did not refuse to confess, but openly declared, "I am not the Christ."
"Then who are you?" they inquired. "Are you Elijah?" He said, "I am not." "Are you the Prophet?" He answered, "No."
So they said to him, "Who are you? We need an answer for those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?"
John replied in the words of Isaiah the prophet: "I am a voice of one calling in the wilderness, 'Make straight the way for the Lord.'"
Then the Pharisees who had been sent
asked him, "Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?"
"I baptize with water," John replied, "but among you stands One you do not know.
He is the One who comes after me, the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie."
All this happened at Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.
The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him and said, "Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!
This is He of whom I said, 'A man who comes after me has surpassed me because He was before me.'
I myself did not know Him, but the reason I came baptizing with water was that He might be revealed to Israel."
Then John testified, "I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove and resting on Him.
I myself did not know Him, but the One who sent me to baptize with water told me, 'The man on whom you see the Spirit descend and rest is He who will baptize with the Holy Spirit.'
I have seen and testified that this is the Son of God."
The next day John was there again with two of his disciples.
When he saw Jesus walking by, he said, "Look, the Lamb of God!"
And when the two disciples heard him say this, they followed Jesus.
Jesus turned and saw them following. "What do you want?" He asked. They said to Him, "Rabbi" (which means Teacher), "where are You staying?"
"Come and see," He replied. So they went and saw where He was staying, and spent that day with Him. It was about the tenth hour.
Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, was one of the two who heard John's testimony and followed Jesus.
He first found his brother Simon and told him, "We have found the Messiah" (which is translated as Christ).
Andrew brought him to Jesus, who looked at him and said, "You are Simon son of John. You will be called Cephas" (which is translated as Peter).
The next day Jesus decided to set out for Galilee. Finding Philip, He told him, "Follow Me."
Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the same town as Andrew and Peter.
Philip found Nathanael and told him, "We have found the One Moses wrote about in the Law, the One the prophets foretold—Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph."
"Can anything good come from Nazareth?" Nathanael asked. "Come and see," said Philip.
When Jesus saw Nathanael approaching, He said of him, "Here is a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit."
"How do You know me?" Nathanael asked. Jesus replied, "Before Philip called you, I saw you under the fig tree."
"Rabbi," Nathanael answered, "You are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!"
Jesus said to him, "Do you believe just because I told you I saw you under the fig tree? You will see greater things than these."
Then He declared, "Truly, truly, I tell you, you will all see heaven open and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man."

context.author: Traditionally the apostle John, son of Zebedee, one of Jesus' innermost three disciples, writing later in life and in a noticeably different style than the other three Gospels
context.genre: Theological narrative — John himself states his purpose plainly near the book's end: "these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God" (20:31), organizing his account around seven chosen "signs" rather than a chronological life story
context.audience: A broad, likely mixed Jewish and Gentile readership toward the end of the first century, written after the other three Gospels and assuming some familiarity with the basic Gospel story already
context.setting: John deliberately opens before Genesis-style time itself, then narrows in on a very specific place: Bethany beyond the Jordan, a different location from the Bethany near Jerusalem, where John the Baptist carried out his baptizing ministry.
context.custom: Rabbis of the era were typically addressed as "Rabbi" by genuine students seeking to learn from them — Nathanael and Andrew's disciples both use the title within their very first exchange with Jesus, signaling they already recognize Him as a teacher worth following.
context.timelineImmediate: This opening chapter moves quickly from a cosmic, pre-creation prologue into concrete, dated events — John the Baptist's testimony, then the calling of the first disciples across just a few consecutive days, ending with Jesus setting out for Galilee.
context.timelineBible: John's opening line, "In the beginning," deliberately echoes Genesis 1:1 word for word, framing everything that follows as a second, greater creation account centered on Jesus as the eternal, active Word of God.
context.sparkNotes: John skips the nativity entirely and opens instead with a cosmic prologue identifying Jesus as the eternal "Word" who was both with God and was God, present at creation itself. From there the chapter moves quickly through John the Baptist's testimony and the calling of the first disciples, closing with Nathanael's confession and Jesus' own promise that "greater things" are still to come.

translation.meaning: In ordinary Greek usage, a word, statement, or reasoned account — John gives it a distinctly new, elevated meaning here, using it specifically as a title for Christ Himself, the very thought and self-expression of God made personal.

occurrences.note: Used hundreds of times throughout the NT for an ordinary word or message — only John uses it, with the definite article, as a direct title for Jesus.

translation.greek: ὁ Ἀμνὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ (ho Amnos tou Theou)
translation.meaning: John the Baptist's declaration draws directly on the Passover lamb and the daily temple sacrifices, presenting Jesus as the sacrifice that actually accomplishes what those symbols could only picture.
"Anointed One" — the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew "Messiah," used here both as John the Baptist's own denial ("I am not the Christ") and Andrew's confession about Jesus.

gospelParallels.note: Matthew's account of John the Baptist's ministry, told from a different angle.
Mark's shorter account of the same events.
Luke's fuller account of John the Baptist's ministry and preaching.

otBackground.note: "In the beginning" — the deliberate opening echo that frames John's whole prologue as a second creation account.
"A voice of one calling in the wilderness" — quoted directly by John the Baptist to describe his own role.
Jacob's ladder, with angels ascending and descending — directly echoed in Jesus' closing promise to Nathanael.

commentary.note: Henry stresses why this opening matters practically, not just doctrinally: 'let none say that when we invite them to Christ we would draw them from God, for Christ is with God and is God.' He reads the light shining in darkness as reaching back before the incarnation itself — the eternal Word already at work in human reason and conscience, long before He took on flesh.

Gill traces 'the Word' back to a real linguistic precedent: the Aramaic Targums (Jewish paraphrases of the Old Testament) frequently used the phrase 'the Memra of the Lord' — 'the Word of the Lord' — as a way of referring to God's own active presence. He argues John is drawing on this existing Jewish tradition directly, not borrowing the idea from Greek philosophy as some critics claimed.

On Nathanael's confession, the early church father Chrysostom reads it as full recognition, not partial: 'Thou art He who was expected, thou art He who was sought for.' He credits Jesus' unexpected knowledge of Nathanael's private moment under the fig tree as proof enough — evidence Nathanael 'could not doubt for an instant.'
